findings.request_raw: GET http://127.0.0.1:3001/#/ (anonymous, pre-login) vs. a freshly-authenticated session for role 'admin'
findings.description: cookie 'cookieconsent_status' is missing the HttpOnly flag -- identified as a session/auth cookie because it was newly issued or changed value across the login boundary for role 'admin'.
findings.recommendation: Set HttpOnly and Secure on every session/auth cookie, and never set SameSite=None without also setting Secure.

findings.vuln_type: Concurrent Session Not Revoked On Re-Login
findings.request_raw: GET http://127.0.0.1:3001/#/ using the FIRST of two independent logins' session cookie for role 'admin', after the second login completed
findings.description: The session cookie captured from a first login for role 'admin' still authenticates against 'http://127.0.0.1:3001/#/' (HTTP 200) after a second, independent login for the same role has completed -- the server does not revoke prior sessions when a new one is established.
findings.recommendation: Either revoke prior sessions when a new authentication event occurs for the same account, or provide the user a way to view and remotely terminate concurrent sessions, per the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet.

findings.request_raw: two independent fresh logins for role 'admin', comparing the 'token' cookie's value each time
findings.response_raw: cookie 'token': two independently-issued tokens for this cookie share an identical 541-character prefix, suggesting a predictable/non-random component
findings.description: Cookie 'token' -- two independently-issued tokens for this cookie share an identical 541-character prefix, suggesting a predictable/non-random component.
findings.recommendation: Generate session identifiers with a cryptographically secure PRNG carrying at least 64 bits of entropy, with no fixed, sequential, or otherwise predictable component, per the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet.

findings.vuln_type: Sensitive Content Cacheable After Logout (Back/Refresh Attack)
findings.response_raw:
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0
findings.description: 'http://127.0.0.1:3001/#/' authenticated response has no Cache-Control: no-store/no-cache directive -- a shared or public browser's back-button/disk cache can replay this authenticated page's content even after the user has logged out.
findings.recommendation: Set Cache-Control: no-store (and Pragma: no-cache for older HTTP/1.0 caches) on every authenticated response.

findings.vuln_type: Missing Rate Limiting At The API/Token Level
findings.response_raw: HTTP 200 on every attempt, no 429/throttling signal observed
findings.description: 6 consecutive authenticated requests to 'http://127.0.0.1:3001/socket.io/?EIO=4&transport=polling&t=Q1g_Jed' produced no HTTP 429 or throttling-shaped response -- this API endpoint has no observable rate limiting at the authenticated/token level, beyond whatever login-only limiting TC-129.3 already checks.
findings.recommendation: Apply per-token/per-account rate limiting to authenticated API endpoints, not just the unauthenticated login endpoint.

findings.vuln_type: Session Not Bound To Client Fingerprint (Hijacking Risk)
findings.request_raw: GET http://127.0.0.1:3001/#/ using role 'admin''s session cookie, with a completely different User-Agent (desktop login vs. mobile replay)
findings.description: The session cookie for role 'admin' is accepted from a client presenting a completely different User-Agent than the one that logged in -- the session is not bound to any client fingerprint, so a stolen cookie alone (no other client secret) is sufficient to hijack the session from a different device/browser.
findings.recommendation: This is a defense-in-depth gap, not a standalone vulnerability (per-request client-binding is unusual and has real usability tradeoffs) -- consider it alongside session lifetime/rotation controls, not as a required fix on its own.

findings.vuln_type: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) / Broken Object Level Authorization (path parameter)
findings.request_raw:
GET http://127.0.0.1:3001/rest/basket/1
GET http://127.0.0.1:3001/rest/basket/2
GET http://127.0.0.1:3001/rest/basket/3
findings.response_raw:
[path segment=1] HTTP 200, 1310 bytes
[path segment=2] HTTP 200, 557 bytes
[path segment=3] HTTP 200, 557 bytes
findings.description: A single authenticated session (role 'admin') retrieved 6 distinct objects from 'http://127.0.0.1:3001/rest/basket/0' by varying its trailing path segment across ['1', '2', '3'], with no apparent server-side ownership check.
findings.recommendation: Enforce object-level authorization on every request that takes an object id from the URL path, not just from query parameters.

findings.vuln_type: Default Configuration -- Missing or Weak Content-Security-Policy
findings.description: 'http://127.0.0.1:3001' no CSP header present (Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8). This is a defense-in-depth gap, not a confirmed exploit path on its own -- it only matters if the application also has an injection point (e.g. reflected/DOM XSS) for a CSP to have blocked, consistent with real disclosed reports of this class (HackerOne #225833) being low-severity precisely because they lacked an actual XSS to chain with.
findings.recommendation: Deploy a strict Content-Security-Policy on every HTML response (e.g. script-src 'self' plus nonces/hashes for any required inline scripts) with no unsafe-inline/unsafe-eval/wildcard sources.

findings.response_raw: <link rel=stylesheet> with path-relative href(s): styles.css, styles.css
findings.description: 'http://127.0.0.1:3001' imports 2 stylesheet(s) using an href relative to the current page's own path rather than the site root: styles.css, styles.css. If this page can ever be rendered at an unexpected/attacker-influenced path (a path-based router, a reflected-path error page), the browser resolves that relative href against the wrong base and can be made to load an attacker-controlled stylesheet from a trusted origin -- a known technique for exfiltrating page content via CSS selectors/attribute readers.
findings.recommendation: Reference stylesheets with a root-relative ('/css/app.css') or absolute (https://...) href, never one relative to the current page's own path.

findings.description: 'http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/Feedbacks/' returned 3 apparent PII value(s) (Email address) in its raw API response.
findings.recommendation: Apply field-level output filtering server-side so an API response never includes more than the calling UI actually needs to render.

findings.response_raw: HTTP 200, sensitive field name(s) present in JSON: password
findings.description: 'http://127.0.0.1:3001/rest/memories/' returns JSON containing internal/sensitive-shaped field name(s) (password) -- consistent with the API serializing an internal model directly rather than an explicit, minimized response shape.
findings.recommendation: Define an explicit response DTO/serializer per endpoint that only includes fields the client actually needs; never serialize an ORM/internal model directly.

findings.response_raw: HTTP 200, 12 file(s) listed: ., quarantine, acquisitions.md, announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, eastere.gg, encrypt.pyc, incident-support.kdbx, legal.md, package-lock.json.bak
findings.description: 'http://127.0.0.1:3001/ftp/' returns a directory listing exposing 12 file(s) (., quarantine, acquisitions.md, announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, eastere.gg, encrypt.pyc, incident-support.kdbx, legal.md, package-lock.json.bak...) -- an attacker gets the exact filenames of everything served from this directory for free, without guessing or brute-forcing, including files nothing on the site links to.
findings.recommendation: Disable directory-listing/autoindexing on the webserver (or the static-file middleware serving this path) so only explicitly-linked files are reachable.

findings.description: Injecting "'" into parameter 'q' (query) on GET http://127.0.0.1:3001/rest/products/search?q= produced a database-error fingerprint ('sqlite_error') in the response (HTTP 500) -- the injected value reached the SQL layer unsanitized. This is a candidate signal only: no data was extracted or altered.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries/prepared statements for every database call; never build SQL from unsanitized request input.

findings.description: Navigating a real browser to http://127.0.0.1:3001/#/?q=%3Cimg+src%3Dx+onerror%3Dconfirm%28%27stofxsse434c4a4%27%29%3E with the marker payload placed in location.hash route query triggered a real confirm() dialog whose message ('stofxsse434c4a4') contains this run's own unique marker -- genuine, confirmed in-browser script execution, not a response-inspection signal. The dialog was auto-dismissed immediately and had no other effect.
findings.recommendation: Never pass location.hash/location.search (or any other client-controlled value) into innerHTML, document.write, eval, or a jQuery selector without HTML-encoding/sanitizing it first; prefer safe DOM APIs (textContent, createElement) for rendering untrusted client-side data.
